claim: Decisions are accompanied by a degree of confidence that a selected option is correct.
source: Decisions are accompanied by a degree of confidence that a selected option is correct.
evidence: This is a foundational statement in the abstract that is supported by the experimental design and results presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: A sequential sampling framework explains the speed and accuracy of decisions.
source: A sequential sampling framework explains the speed and accuracy of decisions and extends naturally to the confidence that the decision rendered is likely to be correct.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the sequential sampling literature and by the model fits to the experimental data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The sequential sampling framework extends naturally to confidence that the decision rendered is likely to be correct.
source: A sequential sampling framework explains the speed and accuracy of decisions and extends naturally to the confidence that the decision rendered is likely to be correct.
evidence: This is supported by the model fits to confidence data in Figure 2 and by previous literature.

claim: Discrepancies between confidence and accuracy suggest that confidence might be supported by mechanisms dissociated from the decision process.
source: However, discrepancies between confidence and accuracy suggest that confidence might be supported by mechanisms dissociated from the decision process.
evidence: This represents a view in the literature that the authors are challenging, supported by citations to other work.

claim: The discrepancy between confidence and accuracy can arise naturally because of simple processing delays.
source: Here we show that this discrepancy can arise naturally because of simple processing delays.
evidence: This is the central claim of the paper, supported by the model fits and psychophysical kernel analyses shown in Figures 3-7.

claim: When participants reported choice and confidence simultaneously, their confidence, reaction time and perceptual decision about motion were explained by bounded evidence accumulation.
source: When participants were asked to report choice and confidence simultaneously, their confidence, reaction time and a perceptual decision about motion were explained by bounded evidence accumulation.
evidence: This is supported by the model fits shown in Figure 2 and Table 1.

claim: Revisions of the initial choice and/or confidence were observed.
source: However, we also observed revisions of the initial choice and/or confidence.
evidence: This is directly observed in the hand trajectory data shown in Figure 1c and quantified in Table 2 and Figure 5.

claim: Changes of mind were explained by a continuation of the mechanism that led to the initial choice.
source: These changes of mind were explained by a continuation of the mechanism that led to the initial choice.
evidence: This is supported by the model fits to change of mind data in Figure 5 and the psychophysical kernel analysis in Figure 4b.

claim: The sequential sampling framework extends to vacillation about confidence.
source: Our findings extend the sequential sampling framework to vacillation about confidence and invites caution in interpreting dissociations between confidence and accuracy.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the paper, supported by the comprehensive modeling and data analysis.

claim: Caution is invited in interpreting dissociations between confidence and accuracy.
source: Our findings extend the sequential sampling framework to vacillation about confidence and invites caution in interpreting dissociations between confidence and accuracy.
evidence: This is supported by the analysis in Figure 7 showing that apparent dissociations can arise from post-decision processing.

claim: Many decisions benefit from the acquisition of multiple samples of evidence acquired sequentially in time.
source: Many decisions benefit from the acquisition of multiple samples of evidence acquired sequentially in time.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by established knowledge in decision-making research.

claim: A decision maker must decide not only about the proposition in question but also about when to terminate deliberation.
source: In that case, a decision maker must decide not only about the proposition in question but also about when to terminate deliberation.
evidence: This is a logical consequence of sequential sampling and is established knowledge in the field.

claim: The tradeoff between speed and accuracy is explained by sequential sampling with optional stopping models in which evidence is accumulated to some stopping criterion or bound.
source: The ensuing tradeoff between speed and accuracy is explained by sequential sampling with optional stopping models in which evidence is accumulated to some stopping criterion or bound (Link, 1975; Ratcliff and Rouder, 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citations to foundational work in the field.

claim: The sequential sampling mechanism receives experimental support from human psychophysics and neural recordings in monkeys and rats.
source: The mechanism receives experimental support from human psychophysics and neural recordings in monkeys and rats (Gold and Shadlen, 2007; Brunton et al., 2013; Shadlen and Kiani, 2013; Hanks et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to empirical studies.

claim: The same framework explains the confidence that a decision is correct.
source: The same framework also explains the confidence that a decision is correct (Kiani and Shadlen, 2009; Kiani et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The decision variable, when combined with elapsed decision time, maps to the probability that a decision rendered on its value will be correct.
source: This is because the quantity that is accumulated, termed a decision variable (DV), when combined with elapsed decision time, maps to the probability that a decision rendered on its value will be correct (Kiani and Shadlen, 2009; Drugowitsch et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical and empirical work.

claim: The attribution of confidence is important for guiding subsequent decisions, learning from mistakes and exploring alternatives.
source: The attribution of confidence is important for guiding subsequent decisions, learning from mistakes and exploring alternatives.
evidence: This is a general statement about the functional importance of confidence, based on established knowledge.

claim: When the decision maker terminates deliberation, the choice is accompanied by a degree of certainty (i.e., confidence), based on the same stream of evidence that supported that decision.
source: Thus, when the decision maker terminates deliberation, the choice is accompanied by a degree of certainty (i.e., confidence), based on the same stream of evidence that supported that decision (Fetsch et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and is a key theoretical claim tested in the paper.

claim: There are many instances when the confidence in a decision and the decision itself are dissociable.
source: This last point remains controversial, however, for there are many instances when the confidence in a decision and the decision itself are dissociable.
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies showing dissociations.

claim: Human decision makers tend to overestimate their certainty about choices based on truly ambiguous evidence.
source: For example, human decision makers tend to overestimate their certainty about choices based on truly ambiguous evidence (Fischoff et al., 1982; Baranski and Petrusic, 1994; Erev et al., 1994; Drugowitsch et al., 2014; Kiani et al., 2014a)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to empirical studies.

claim: Decision makers can perform above chance level yet report they are guessing.
source: and they can perform above chance level yet report they are guessing (Kunimoto et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to an empirical study.

claim: These observations have led psychologists to suggest that confidence and choice may be guided by different sources of evidence.
source: These and other observations have led psychologists to suggest that confidence and choice may be guided by different sources of evidence (Pleskac and Busemeyer, 2010; Zylberberg et al., 2012; Moran et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical work proposing dissociations.

claim: The evaluation of the same evidence differs fundamentally in the way that it affects choice and confidence.
source: or that the evaluation of the same evidence differs fundamentally in the way that it affects choice and confidence (Fleming and Dolan, 2012; Maniscalco and Lau, 2012; De Martino et al., 2013; Ratcliff and Starns, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to theoretical and empirical work.

claim: The distinction between 1st-order and 2nd-order confidence is captured by the notion that 1st-order confidence is based rationally on the evidence in support of the decision and 2nd-order confidence can depart from this evidence.
source: The latter distinction is captured by the notion of a 1st-order confidence that is based rationally on the evidence in support of the decision and a 2nd-order confidence that can depart from this evidence.
evidence: This is a theoretical distinction from the metacognition literature.

claim: It is possible that some of the observations taken as support for higher order explanations of confidence are simply accounted for by deficiencies of the theory of 1st order choices.
source: As this distinction rests on a proper understanding of the mechanism that supports choice and confidence, it is possible that some of the observations taken as support for higher order explanations of confidence are simply accounted for by deficiencies of the theory of 1st order choices.
evidence: This is a speculative claim that motivates the current study.

claim: If a decision maker acquires additional information after committing to a choice, she might wish to revise a decision, or the confidence in that decision, or both.
source: Naturally, if a decision maker acquires additional information after committing to a choice, she might wish to revise a decision, or the confidence in that decision, or both.
evidence: This is a logical inference about decision-making behavior.

claim: Changes of mind occur occasionally, even when there appears to be no additional information available after the initial decision has been rendered.
source: Such changes of mind occur occasionally, even when there appears to be no additional information available after the initial decision has been rendered.
evidence: This is an empirical observation from the literature and the current study.

claim: The sequential sampling framework offers a natural account of changes of mind because the mechanism incorporates processing delays, which leave open the possibility that the brain might have access to additional evidence that did not influence the initial decision.
source: The sequential sampling framework (e.g., bounded evidence accumulation) offers a natural account of this phenomenon, because the mechanism incorporates processing delays, which leave open the possibility that the brain might have access to additional evidence that did not influence the initial decision and which might instead influence a revision.
evidence: This is a theoretical claim that is tested in the paper.

claim: Evidence for a process involving processing delays was adduced to explain reversals of perceptual decisions in humans and monkeys.
source: Evidence for such a process was adduced to explain reversals of perceptual decisions in humans and monkeys (Rabbitt, 1966; Rabbitt and Vyas, 1981; McPeek et al., 2000; Caspi and Beutter, 2004; Van Zandt and Maldonado-Molina, 2004; Resulaj et al., 2009; Burk et al., 2014; Kiani et al., 2014b; Moher and Song, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to empirical studies.

claim: The same mechanism that accounts for changes of decision can account for a revision in the confidence a decision maker assigns to his or her choice.
source: Here, we address the possibility that this same mechanism can account for a revision in the confidence a decision maker assigns to his or her choice.
evidence: This is the central hypothesis of the paper, tested with the experimental data.

claim: Revisions of confidence might account for an apparent dissociation between degree of confidence and choice.
source: We hypothesized that such revisions might account for an apparent dissociation between degree of confidence and choice.
evidence: This is a hypothesis tested in the paper, particularly in Figure 7.

claim: Four subjects performed the motion direction discrimination task.
source: Four subjects performed the motion direction discrimination task illustrated in Figure 1a.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: The stimulus duration was controlled by the subjects.
source: The stimulus duration was controlled by the subjects (Figure 1b), who were trained to make fast but accurate decisions (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: Subjects were trained to make fast but accurate decisions.
source: The stimulus duration was controlled by the subjects (Figure 1b), who were trained to make fast but accurate decisions (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental procedure.

claim: Subjects moved a handle from the home position to one of four choice targets, thereby indicating simultaneously the direction decision and confidence level.
source: Whenever ready, the subject moved a handle from the home position to one of four choice targets, thereby indicating simultaneously the direction decision and confidence level.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: On most trials subjects made an approximately straight-line movement to one of the choice targets.
source: On most trials subjects made an approximately straight-line movement to one of the choice targets.
evidence: This is an empirical observation from the hand trajectory data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: The random dot stimulus was extinguished on movement onset.
source: However, although the random dot stimulus was extinguished on movement onset, on a proportion of trials subjects changed their choice or confidence rating or both, initially reaching towards one target but deviating to reach another (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: On a proportion of trials subjects changed their choice or confidence rating or both, initially reaching towards one target but deviating to reach another.
source: However, although the random dot stimulus was extinguished on movement onset, on a proportion of trials subjects changed their choice or confidence rating or both, initially reaching towards one target but deviating to reach another (Figure 1c).
evidence: This is an empirical observation shown in Figure 1c and quantified in Table 2.

claim: A common mechanism explains the rate of changes of mind, as well as the speed, accuracy and confidence in the subjects' initial decisions.
source: Our central hypothesis is that a common mechanism explains the rate of these occurrences, as well as the speed, accuracy and confidence in the subjects' initial decisions.
evidence: This is the central hypothesis of the paper, supported by the model fits in Figures 2 and 5.

claim: Stronger motion supported more accurate decisions.
source: Not surprisingly, stronger motion supported more accurate (Figure 2a) and faster decisions (Figure 2b), that tended to be assigned the higher confidence (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2a.

claim: Stronger motion supported faster decisions.
source: Not surprisingly, stronger motion supported more accurate (Figure 2a) and faster decisions (Figure 2b), that tended to be assigned the higher confidence (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2b.

claim: Stronger motion tended to be assigned higher confidence.
source: Not surprisingly, stronger motion supported more accurate (Figure 2a) and faster decisions (Figure 2b), that tended to be assigned the higher confidence (Figure 2c).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2c.

claim: When subjects were more confident, they tended to be more accurate.
source: When subjects were more confident, they tended to be more accurate (Figure 2a; P<0.0001 for all subjects) and faster (Figure 2b; P<0.0001 for all subjects).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2a with statistical significance reported.

claim: When subjects were more confident, they tended to be faster.
source: When subjects were more confident, they tended to be more accurate (Figure 2a; P<0.0001 for all subjects) and faster (Figure 2b; P<0.0001 for all subjects).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2b with statistical significance reported.

claim: Subjects reported high confidence more often on correct choices than on errors.
source: In addition, subjects reported high confidence more often on correct choices than on errors (Figure 2c)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2c.

claim: Subjects tended to be more confident on those errors associated with stronger motion.
source: and they tended to be more confident on those errors associated with stronger motion (P<1e-5 for 3 subjects and P = 0.50 for S3).
evidence: This is an empirical observation with statistical significance reported.

claim: The regularities in choice, confidence, and reaction time are consistent with a common mechanism of bounded evidence accumulation.
source: These regularities are consistent with a common mechanism of bounded evidence accumulation to support choice, reaction time and confidence (Kiani et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by the model fits shown in Figure 2 and by citation to previous work.

claim: The process involves a race between a mechanism that accumulates evidence for right, and against left, and a process that integrates evidence for left, and against right.
source: The process involves a race between a mechanism that accumulates evidence for right, and against left, and a process that integrates evidence for left, and against right (Usher and McClelland, 2001; Mazurek et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a description of the model architecture, supported by citations.

claim: The two accumulation processes obtain evidence originating in the same stimulus and will tend to accumulate noisy evidence of opposite sign (i.e., anti-correlated).
source: Since these processes obtain evidence originating in the same stimulus, they will tend to accumulate noisy evidence of opposite sign (i.e., anti-correlated).
evidence: This is a logical consequence of the model architecture.

claim: The neural noise associated with the accumulations need not be perfectly anticorrelated.
source: However, the neural noise associated with the accumulations need not be perfectly anticorrelated, so they are depicted separately (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is a statement about the model assumptions, illustrated in Figure 3a.

claim: The first process to reach an upper bound determines the choice and decision time.
source: The first process to reach an upper bound determines the choice and decision time.
evidence: This is a core feature of the bounded accumulation model.

claim: The degree of belief is based on the balance of evidence (i.e., difference) between winning and losing DVs, as well as the decision time.
source: Thus the degree of belief is based on the balance of evidence (i.e., difference) between winning and losing DVs, as well as the decision time.
evidence: This is a description of how confidence is computed in the model.

claim: This model has been tested in neurophysiology and a previous report in humans.
source: This model has been tested in neurophysiology and a previous report in humans (Kiani et al., 2014a) which extends ideas from signal detection theory, race, and Bayesian models (Vickers, 1979; Kepecs et al., 2008; Maniscalco and Lau, 2012; Drugowitsch et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to empirical and theoretical work.

claim: The main distinction of the model is the recognition that the time to decision influences confidence.
source: Its main distinction is the recognition that the time to decision influences confidence (Fetsch et al., 2014; Kiani et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The time to decision influences confidence explains why confidence associated with errors increases with stronger coherences: stronger motion induces faster decision times for correct and errors alike.
source: For example, this explains why confidence associated with errors increases with stronger coherences: stronger motion induces faster decision times for correct and errors alike.
evidence: This is an inference from the model that is consistent with the data in Figure 2c.

claim: Subjects adopt a consistent criterion on "degree of belief" (log odds) to decide in favor of high or low confidence.
source: For simplicity, we assumed that subjects adopt a consistent criterion on "degree of belief" (log odds, Figure 3b) to decide in favor of high or low confidence.
evidence: This is a model assumption illustrated in Figure 3b.

claim: The model captures the main features of the subjects' choices.
source: The smooth curves in Figure 2 are fits of the model (4 parameters; see Materials and methods), which capture the main features of the subjects' choices.
evidence: This is shown by the model fits in Figure 2.

claim: Subjects differed in their sensitivity, speed/accuracy and confidence which was accounted for by the parameters of the fits.
source: Naturally, subjects differed in their sensitivity, speed/accuracy and confidence which was accounted for by the parameters of the fits (Table 1).
evidence: This is shown in Table 1.

claim: Subjects differed in their criteria for categorizing degree of belief into high and low, which can be appreciated by the separation of choice functions by confidence report.
source: They also differed in their criteria for categorizing degree of belief into high and low, which can be appreciated by the separation of choice functions by confidence report.
evidence: This is an observation from Figure 2 and the model fits.

claim: To maximize the number of points, given the reward structure, subjects should choose high confidence if they believe the probability of a correct choice is greater than two-thirds, which corresponds to a log-odds of 0.69.
source: To maximize the number of points, given the reward structure (see Materials and methods), subjects should choose high confidence if they believe the probability of a correct choice is greater than two-thirds, which corresponds to a log-odds of 0.69.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the reward structure described in the methods.

claim: The inferred criteria for all the subjects were close to the optimal criterion, although all subjects were somewhat risk-averse.
source: Interestingly the inferred criteria for all the subjects were close to this optimal criterion, although all subjects were somewhat risk-averse (probability thresholds of 0.71, 0.78, 0.71 and 0.75; thresholds in log-odd units shown in Table 1).
evidence: This is based on the model fits shown in Table 1.

claim: There are some noteworthy discrepancies between model and data (e.g., proportion of high confidence choices at 0% coherence for 3 of 4 subjects).
source: There are some noteworthy discrepancies between model and data (e.g., proportion of high confidence choices at 0% coherence for 3 of 4 subjects)
evidence: This is an observation from comparing the model fits to the data in Figure 2.

claim: The model captures the trend in the confidence ratings on error trials for 3 of 4 subjects, even though the fits themselves are dominated by the more numerous correct choices.
source: but the model captures the trend in the confidence ratings on error trials, mentioned above (3 of 4 subjects; Figure 2c), even though the fits themselves are dominated by the more numerous correct choices.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2c.

claim: The model is vastly superior to two alternative formulations, which would explain confidence on balance of evidence or deliberation time but not both.
source: The model is vastly superior to two alternative formulations, which would explain confidence on balance of evidence or deliberation time but not both (compared to the original model, log likelihood is reduced by 63–1180 and 2301–3749 across participants for these models, respectively; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is based on model comparison statistics.

claim: The fits of the initial choices allow characterization of the state of the DV—including decision time—leading to the subjects' choice and the mapping of this DV to confidence.
source: Importantly, the fits of the initial choices allow us to characterize the state of the DV—including decision time—leading to the subjects' choice and the mapping of this DV to confidence.
evidence: This is a statement about what the model fits provide.

claim: The same information was used to reach an initial choice about direction and confidence.
source: The critical assumptions are (i) the same information was used to reach an initial choice about direction and confidence, and (ii) there is additional information available to the decision maker after committing to a choice and confidence category, despite the disappearance of the random dot motion upon response initiation.
evidence: This is a critical assumption of the model, supported by the psychophysical kernel analysis in Figure 4a.

claim: There is additional information available to the decision maker after committing to a choice and confidence category, despite the disappearance of the random dot motion upon response initiation.
source: The critical assumptions are (i) the same information was used to reach an initial choice about direction and confidence, and (ii) there is additional information available to the decision maker after committing to a choice and confidence category, despite the disappearance of the random dot motion upon response initiation.
evidence: This is a critical assumption of the model, supported by the psychophysical kernel analysis in Figure 4.

claim: Both assumptions are supported by the model-free analyses depicted in Figure 4.
source: Both assumptions are supported by the model-free analyses depicted in Figure 4.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4.

claim: The similar time course of the confidence and choice kernels implies that the initial direction and confidence choices were supported by a common evidence stream.
source: The similar time course of the confidence and choice kernels implies that the initial direction and confidence choices were supported by a common evidence stream.
evidence: This is an inference from the psychophysical kernel analysis shown in Figure 4a.

claim: Subjects relied on information from the beginning of the display until ~400 ms before movement onset to guide both their direction choices and their confidence.
source: Moreover, by discounting the lag and smoothing introduced by the motion filter (inset), it is apparent that subjects relied on information from the beginning of the display until ~400 ms before movement onset (arrows; see Materials and methods and Figure 4—figure supplement 1) to guide both their direction choices and their confidence.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4a and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The estimates of information cutoff time are consistent with the estimates of non-decision time (tnd) obtained from the model fits to the initial choices and RTs.
source: These values are consistent with the estimates of non-decision time (tnd) obtained from the model fits to the initial choices and RTs (Table 1).
evidence: This is a comparison between the psychophysical kernel analysis and the model fits shown in Table 1.

claim: Some of the additional ~400 ms of information, which did not inform the initial direction and confidence choices, affects changes of mind about direction, confidence or both.
source: We next evaluate our hypothesis that some of the additional ~400 ms of information, which did not inform the initial direction and confidence choices, affects changes of mind about direction, confidence or both.
evidence: This is the hypothesis tested with the change of mind data in Figures 4b and 5.

claim: After indicating their initial choices, subjects occasionally changed the direction of their hand movement to indicate a different direction or level of confidence or both.
source: After indicating their initial choices, subjects occasionally changed the direction of their hand movement to indicate a different direction or level of confidence or both (Table 2 and Figure 5).
evidence: This is shown in Table 2 and Figure 5.

claim: The frequency of changes of mind varied between subjects, from 2.0 to 8.8% of trials.
source: The frequency of these changes of mind varied between subjects, from 2.0 to 8.8% of trials.
evidence: This is shown in Table 2.

claim: Changes of decision were more likely if the initial decision was an error than if it was correct.
source: Changes of decision were more likely if the initial decision was an error than if it was correct (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5a.

claim: Corrections of initial errors were more likely if the motion information was stronger.
source: These corrections were more likely if the motion information was stronger.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5a.

claim: For three of the four subjects, changes of decision corrected an initial error more often than they spoiled an initially correct choice.
source: For three of the four subjects, changes of decision corrected an initial error more often than they spoiled an initially correct choice (P<0.001, P<0.001, P = 0.084, P<0.001), consistent with previous reports (Resulaj et al., 2009; Burk et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an empirical observation with statistical significance reported and supported by citations.

claim: For all subjects, changes of confidence were more frequent than changes of decision.
source: For all subjects, changes of confidence were more frequent than changes of decision (Table 2 and Figure 5c; p<1e-4 for all participants).
evidence: This is shown in Table 2 and Figure 5c with statistical significance reported.

claim: Changes of confidence were more likely if the initial decision was low confidence than if it was high confidence.
source: Further, changes of confidence were more likely if the initial decision was low confidence than if it was high confidence (Figure 5b).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Changes to high confidence were more likely when the initial low confidence accompanied a stronger motion.
source: These changes to high confidence were more likely when the initial low confidence accompanied a stronger motion.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5b.

claim: Changes of mind were beneficial to the participants in that on changes of mind trials the gain in points over not changing one's mind ranged from 0.72–1.12 points across the subjects.
source: Changes of mind were beneficial to the participants in that on changes of mind trials (either decision, confidence or both) the gain in points over not changing one's mind ranged from 0.72–1.12 points across the subjects (Table 2).
evidence: This is shown in Table 2.

claim: Changes of both decision and confidence were less common (0.4–1.6%), which may be partly due to an energy cost associated with crossing the workspace.
source: Changes of both decision and confidence were less common (0.4–1.6%), which may be partly due to an energy cost associated with crossing the workspace (Burk et al., 2014; Moher and Song, 2014).
evidence: This is an empirical observation with a speculative explanation supported by citations.

claim: Double changes that did occur tended to move from high to low confidence compared to trials from low to high.
source: Those double changes that did occur tended to move from high to low confidence (1.03, 0.35, 0.12, 1.36%) compared to trials from low to high (0.26, 0.04, 0.04, 0.26%; p<0.0001 for three subjects and p<0.05 for S3).
evidence: This is an empirical observation with statistical significance reported.

claim: A change of confidence, like a change of decision, can be explained by continuation of the processing of visual information that arrived after the subject had committed to her initial choice.
source: We hypothesized that a change of confidence, like a change of decision, can be explained by continuation of the processing of visual information that arrived after the subject had committed to her initial choice (Figure 3b).
evidence: This is the hypothesis tested with the model shown in Figure 3b and the data in Figures 4b and 5.

claim: When subjects changed their confidence rating from low to high, the motion information in the post-decision period supported the initial choice.
source: Indeed, when subjects changed their confidence rating from low to high, the motion information in the post-decision period supported the initial choice (Figure 4b, bottom)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4b, bottom panel.

claim: Changes from high to low confidence were associated with motion information in support of the direction opposite to the one chosen.
source: whereas changes from high to low confidence were associated with motion information in support of the direction opposite to the one chosen (Figure 4b, middle)
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4b, middle panel.

claim: The trend of motion information supporting changes was amplified for changes of mind about direction.
source: and this trend was amplified for changes of mind about direction (Figure 4b, top).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4b, top panel.

claim: A simple extension of the bounded accumulation model explains the frequency of changes of mind as well as their dependency on features of the stimulus and the subject's initial report.
source: A simple extension of the bounded accumulation model explains the frequency of these changes as well as their dependency on features of the stimulus and the subject's initial report.
evidence: This is supported by the model fits shown in Figure 5.

claim: Evidence was accumulated past the point of the initial decision for a fixed amount of time (tpip) that is less than the non-decision time.
source: We assumed that evidence was accumulated past the point of the initial decision for a fixed amount of time (a free parameter, tpip) that is less than the non-decision time.
evidence: This is a model assumption.

claim: The state of the belief at tpip determines the final confidence and choice.
source: The state of the belief at tpip determines the final confidence and choice (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a model assumption.

claim: Subjects might not apply the identical criteria for confidence and choice in the pre- and post-initiation epoch.
source: As shown in Figure 3b, we allowed for the possibility that subjects might not apply the identical criteria for confidence and choice in the pre- and post-initiation epoch (the δθ parameters; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a model assumption illustrated in Figure 3b.

claim: The settings of tpip and the δθ parameters capture aspects of the energetic costs, by suppressing changes that would occur with small fluctuations in the evidence or very late in the movement.
source: The settings of tpip and the δθ parameters capture aspects of the energetic costs, by suppressing changes that would occur with small fluctuations in the evidence or very late in the movement.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model parameters.

claim: The model fits capture the main features of the subjects' revisions of both choice and confidence.
source: The curves in Figure 5 are fits of the model, which capture the main features of the subjects' revisions of both choice and confidence.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5.

claim: All parameters of the change of mind model fits are fixed from the fits to the initial choice and confidence, except for the three δθ parameters and tpip.
source: Note that all parameters of these fits are fixed from the fits to the initial choice and confidence, except for the three δθ parameters and tpip (fit values in Table 1).
evidence: This is a statement about the model fitting procedure, with values shown in Table 1.

claim: The variations in the participants' behavior are accounted for by the different settings of the model parameters.
source: The variations in the participants' behavior are accounted for by the different settings of the model parameters, which are illustrated graphically in Figure 6 for an initial low and initial high confidence rightward decision.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6.

claim: After an initial low confidence decision, all subjects required more belief to change to a high confidence decision than would have been required for an initial high confidence decision (δθ1>0).
source: After an initial low confidence decision (Figure 6, top row), all subjects required more belief to change to a high confidence decision than would have been required for an initial high confidence decision (δθ1>0).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6 and Table 1.

claim: Similar hysteresis is seen for initial high confidence decisions.
source: Similar hysteresis is seen for initial high confidence decisions (Figure 6, bottom row).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 6.

claim: All subjects required more evidence to change their initial decision about direction than a simple reversal in sign of the evidence (δθ2>0).
source: Moreover, all subjects required more evidence to change their initial decision about direction than a simple reversal in sign of the evidence (δθ2>0).
evidence: This is shown in Table 1.

claim: All participants relaxed their belief criterion when they changed their direction decision while either maintaining or changing to high confidence (δθ3<0).
source: Finally, all participants relaxed their belief criterion when they changed their direction decision while either maintaining or changing to high confidence (δθ3<0).
evidence: This is shown in Table 1.

claim: Because most initial choices were high confidence, the strategy of relaxing the belief criterion for double changes would reduce motor effort by avoiding changes of both direction and confidence, as this requires crossing the workspace with a complete reversal of the initial movement.
source: Because most initial choices were high confidence, this strategy would reduce motor effort by avoiding changes of both direction and confidence, as this requires crossing the workspace with a complete reversal of the initial movement.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the model parameters in relation to motor costs.

claim: Confidence and direction reports remain coupled via a common mechanism at the time of both the initial and final decision.
source: We wish to emphasize that confidence and direction reports remain coupled via a common mechanism at the time of both the initial and final decision.
evidence: This is a key conclusion supported by the model fits and psychophysical kernel analyses.

claim: The observation supports a parsimonious account of decision confidence which is somewhat at odds with recent literature on meta-cognition.
source: The observation supports a parsimonious account of decision confidence which is somewhat at odds with recent literature on meta-cognition (see Discussion).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the results.

claim: Evidence for a meta-cognitive process is adduced from a dissociation between the signal-to-noise properties of the evidence that would support a level of choice accuracy versus the level associated with a degree of confidence (e.g., meta-d′).
source: Evidence for a meta-cognitive process is adduced from a dissociation between the signal-to-noise properties of the evidence that would support a level of choice accuracy versus the level associated with a degree of confidence (e.g., meta-d′; see Fleming and Lau, 2014; Maniscalco and Lau, 2012).
evidence: This is a description of the meta-cognition literature, supported by citations.

claim: The meta-d′ statistic is not well behaved in the sequential sampling framework, but the basic logic remains applicable.
source: The meta-d′ statistic is not well behaved in the sequential sampling framework, but the basic logic remains applicable (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a statement about the applicability of meta-d′ to the current framework.

claim: There is a systematic discrepancy between the odds ratios calculated from initial versus final confidence ratings.
source: In Figure 7, we compare two odds ratios (OR). Both express the relative probability of a high-confidence rating, given a correct or error choice. Along the abscissa, we base the OR on the initial confidence ratings, whereas on the ordinate, we use the final confidence ratings, thus accommodating the change of confidence. In essence, we are pretending that the subject indicated her choice and subsequently told us her confidence. Clearly, there is a systematic discrepancy between the OR pairs (P<1e-4, sign test).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7 with statistical significance reported.

claim: All but one of the odds ratio points are above the main diagonal.
source: All but one of the points are above the main diagonal, and the difference in OR is statistically reliable for 13 of the 19 individual points (4 subjects × 5 non-zero motion strengths with at least 1 error; P<0.05, bootstrap; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7 with statistical significance reported.

claim: The difference in odds ratio is statistically reliable for 13 of the 19 individual points.
source: All but one of the points are above the main diagonal, and the difference in OR is statistically reliable for 13 of the 19 individual points (4 subjects × 5 non-zero motion strengths with at least 1 error; P<0.05, bootstrap; see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the bootstrap analysis.

claim: The discrepancy in odds ratios might be regarded as a sign of 2nd-order confidence, whereas it is simply the result of a continuation of the 1st-order process that couples choice and confidence, via bounded evidence accumulation.
source: This discrepancy might be regarded as a sign of 2nd-order confidence, whereas it is simply the result of a continuation of the 1st-order process that couples choice and confidence, via bounded evidence accumulation.
evidence: This is the key conclusion from the odds ratio analysis in Figure 7.

claim: Confidence is perhaps the most important and the least understood manifestation of choice behavior compared to speed and accuracy.
source: Amongst the three manifestations of choice behavior, confidence is perhaps the most important and the least understood—compared to speed and accuracy
evidence: This is a general statement about the state of the field.

claim: In the world outside the laboratory, we do not always receive immediate feedback about our choices.
source: because in the world outside the laboratory, we do not always receive immediate feedback about our choices.
evidence: This is a general observation about real-world decision-making.

claim: Often, all we know about the accuracy of a choice is a degree of confidence.
source: Often, all we know about the accuracy of a choice is a degree of confidence.
evidence: This is a general observation about the role of confidence in decision-making.

claim: The present study establishes that the assessment of confidence evolves in time and, like the choice itself, can undergo revision with additional evidence.
source: The present study establishes that this assessment evolves in time and, like the choice itself, can undergo revision with additional evidence.
evidence: This is a key conclusion of the study, supported by the data on changes of confidence.

claim: The study of perceptual decision-making offers insight into the confidence process because the stream of evidence can be controlled experimentally.
source: The study of perceptual decision-making offers insight into the process because the stream of evidence can be controlled experimentally.
evidence: This is a statement about the advantages of the experimental approach.

claim: In the present study using random dot kinematograms, the temporal stream of evidence is effectively a sequence of independent, statistically stationary samples.
source: This is especially so in the present study using random dot kinematograms because the temporal stream of evidence is effectively a sequence of independent, statistically stationary samples.
evidence: This is a statement about the properties of the stimulus used in the study.

claim: In other types of decisions, the samples of evidence are derived from internal evaluations and memory processes, which are less well characterized, but which also evolve as a function of time.
source: In other types of decisions—and most perceptual ones as well—the samples of evidence are derived from internal evaluations and memory processes, which are less well characterized, but which also evolve as a function of time.
evidence: This is a general statement about other types of decisions.

claim: The class of bounded sequential sampling models explains the tradeoff between speed and accuracy, and many of the essential steps have correlates in neurophysiology.
source: The class of bounded sequential sampling models, including many variants (Wald, 1947; Stone, 1960; Laming, 1968; Link, 1975; Good, 1979; Luce, 1986; Ratcliff and Rouder, 1998) explains the tradeoff between speed and accuracy, and many of the essential steps have correlates in neurophysiology (Romo et al., 2002; Heekeren et al., 2004; Ploran et al., 2007; Heitz and Schall, 2012; White et al., 2012; Kelly and O'Connell, 2013; Hanks et al., 2014; Hanks et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to theoretical and empirical work.

claim: The mechanism exposes a discrepancy between the information supplied to the decision maker and the information that is actually used to make the decision.
source: The mechanism (and models) also expose a discrepancy between the information supplied to the decision maker and the information that is actually used to make the decision.
evidence: This is a key insight from the sequential sampling framework.

claim: There are processing delays between the arrival of information from the environment and updating its representation in working memory as a decision variable bearing on a proposition.
source: Specifically, there are processing delays between the arrival of information from the environment and updating its representation in working memory as a decision variable bearing on a proposition
evidence: This is a statement about sensory processing delays.

claim: There are delays between commitment to a decision and communicating this decision through the motor system.
source: and there are delays between commitment to a decision and communicating this decision through the motor system.
evidence: This is a statement about motor processing delays.

claim: Even in relatively fast perceptual decisions, the non-decision time typically exceeds 300 ms.
source: Even in relatively fast perceptual decisions, this so-called non-decision time typically exceeds 300 ms.
evidence: This is a general statement about non-decision times, consistent with the estimates in Table 1.

claim: In previous studies, the motor system receives a continuous updating of the state of the evidence leading to a choice.
source: In previous studies, we showed that the motor system receives a continuous updating of the state of the evidence leading to a choice (Gold and Shadlen, 2000; Selen et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The motor system can utilize the late arriving information to revise an initial choice by continuing the process of deliberation.
source: and can utilize the late arriving information to revise an initial choice by continuing the process of deliberation (Resulaj et al., 2009; Burk et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The present study extends observations about changes of decision to the metacognitive operation of assigning a degree of belief that the decision is correct.
source: The present study extends these observations to the metacognitive operation of assigning a degree of belief that the decision is correct.
evidence: This is a key conclusion of the study.

claim: Deliberation in the post-initiation epoch is as rich a process as the deliberation preceding initiation.
source: First, it establishes that deliberation in the post-initiation epoch is as rich a process as the deliberation preceding initiation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the results on changes of confidence and decision.

claim: Termination has a kind of specificity; it marks the end of deliberation for purposes of response initiation, but it does not actually terminate all deliberation.
source: This implies that termination has a kind of specificity; it marks the end of deliberation for purposes of response initiation, but it does not actually terminate all deliberation.
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that deliberation continues after response initiation.

claim: The same information can bear on a variety of potential actions and cognitive operations, which need not share identical speed-accuracy tradeoffs and thus deliberate for different amounts of time.
source: For example, the same information can bear on a variety of potential actions and cognitive operations, which need not share identical speed-accuracy tradeoffs and thus deliberate for different amounts of time.
evidence: This is a speculative extension of the findings.

claim: The finding explains a potential dissociation between the information that decision makers might use to guide confidence and choice.
source: Second, the finding explains a potential dissociation between the information that decision makers might use to guide confidence and choice.
evidence: This is a key conclusion of the study, particularly from Figure 7.

claim: The initial choice and confidence are explained using the identical stream of information, as in a previous study.
source: We explain the initial choice and confidence using the identical stream of information, as in a previous study (Kiani et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is supported by the model fits in Figure 2 and the psychophysical kernel analysis in Figure 4a.

claim: On many trials, the final confidence judgments are clearly based on additional information that did not affect the initial choice.
source: The model is by no means perfect (e.g., it overestimates confidence at the lowest motion strength), but it demonstrates, nonetheless, that on many trials, the final confidence judgments are clearly based on additional information that did not affect the initial choice.
evidence: This is supported by the psychophysical kernel analysis in Figure 4b and the model fits in Figure 5.

claim: The assertion that final confidence is based on additional information is supported by the analysis of motion energy leading to the confidence choices.
source: This assertion is supported by the analysis of motion energy leading to the confidence choices (Figure 4).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4.

claim: Just a few hundred milliseconds of additional evidence led to changes in the confidence associated with the initial choice, ranging from 1.5–6.3% of trials across subjects.
source: Just a few hundred milliseconds of additional evidence led to changes in the confidence associated with the initial choice, ranging from 1.5–6.3% of trials across our subjects
evidence: This is based on the data in Table 2.

claim: The additional evidence was enough to induce a clear departure from the level of confidence that ought to be associated with the evidence available at the time of the initial choice.
source: and this was enough to induce a clear departure from the level of confidence that ought to be associated with the evidence available at the time of the initial choice.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 7.

claim: Had subjects been asked only for their confidence rating after they indicated their initial choice—without an opportunity to revise those choices—a different relationship between confidence and accuracy would have been detected.
source: In other words, had we asked our subjects only for their confidence rating after they indicated their initial choice—without an opportunity to revise those choices—we would have detected a different relationship between confidence and accuracy (Figure 7).
evidence: This is demonstrated in Figure 7.

claim: When confidence is assessed after the initial choice, as it is in most experiments, then it ought to come as no surprise that choice and confidence are explained by only partially overlapping sources of information.
source: When confidence is assessed after the initial choice, as it is in most experiments, then it ought to come as no surprise that choice and confidence are explained by only partially overlapping sources of information.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the results.

claim: The observation that choice and confidence are explained by partially overlapping sources of information does not imply a dissociation between confidence and the decision, as the latter can also be revised based on the same additional information.
source: Importantly, however, this does not imply a dissociation between confidence and the decision (Pleskac and Busemeyer, 2010), as the latter can also be revised based on the same additional information.
evidence: This is a key conclusion of the study.

claim: In many settings, it is possible that a decision maker might acquire new information after an initial choice, either from the environment or from memory, and this could lead to a divergence of choice and confidence.
source: Of course, in many settings, it is possible that a decision maker might acquire new information after an initial choice, either from the environment or from memory (e.g., reconsidering the evidence, weights and costs), and this could lead to a divergence of choice and confidence.
evidence: This is a general statement about other possible sources of dissociation.

claim: The result invites caution when interpreting divergence between choice and confidence as indicators of metacognitive processes.
source: However, our result invites caution when interpreting such divergence as indicators of metacognitive processes.
evidence: This is a key conclusion of the study.

claim: The central question is whether additional information affects confidence in a manner that is fundamentally different from the process that would tie these attributes together.
source: The central question is whether this additional information affects confidence in a manner that is fundamentally different from the process that would tie these attributes together.
evidence: This is a statement of the key question addressed by the study.

claim: In the current study, the answer to whether additional information affects confidence in a fundamentally different manner seems to be negative.
source: In our study, the answer seems to be negative
evidence: This is the conclusion from the study.

claim: The interesting aspects of more real-world distinctions involving re-evaluation of evidence using memory will require better understanding of the way that memory and decision processes interact but not a fundamentally different mechanism for associating confidence with the evidence arising from that process.
source: and we speculate that the interesting aspects of more real-world distinctions involving re-evaluation of evidence using memory, for example, will require better understanding of the way that memory and decision processes interact but not a fundamentally different mechanism for associating confidence with the evidence arising from that process.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research directions.

claim: Confidence, choice and reaction time can be understood in a common framework of bounded evidence accumulation.
source: We conclude that confidence, choice and reaction time can be understood in a common framework of bounded evidence accumulation.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by all the results.

claim: By definition, confidence may be regarded as metacognitive, simply because it is a report about the decision process itself.
source: By definition, confidence may be regarded as metacognitive, simply because it is a report about the decision process itself.
evidence: This is a definitional statement.

claim: The operations leading to confidence seem neither mysterious nor dissociable from the decision process.
source: Yet the operations leading to confidence seem neither mysterious nor dissociable from the decision process (cf. De Martino et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study.

claim: There are many unknown features of the underlying mechanism of confidence.
source: That said, there are many unknown features of the underlying mechanism.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of limitations.

claim: We know little about the establishment of the mapping between belief and the representation of evidence and time.
source: We know little about the establishment of the mapping between belief and the representation of evidence and time.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of what is not known.

claim: We do not know how a criterion is applied to the mapping between belief and evidence to render categorical choices or confidence ratings.
source: Nor do we know how a criterion is applied to this mapping to render the categorical choices in our study, or in post-decision wagering decisions (Kiani and Shadlen, 2009), or in confidence ratings (Maniscalco and Lau, 2012; Fleming and Lau, 2014; Kiani et al., 2014a).
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of what is not known, with citations to relevant work.

claim: An appealing idea is that the application of a criterion also looks like a threshold crossing in the brain with dynamic costs associated with time (e.g., urgency) and dynamic biases.
source: An appealing idea is that this also looks like a threshold crossing in the brain with dynamic costs associated with time (e.g., urgency Thura et al., 2012; Drugowitsch et al., 2012) and dynamic biases (Hanks et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a speculative idea supported by citations.

claim: Downstream structures that represent confidence-related values such as reward prediction error must approximate the mapping between decision variable and elapsed time to achieve confidence representation.
source: Presumably, downstream structures that represent confidence-related values such as reward prediction error, must approximate the mapping between decision variable—represented in LIP and other brain areas—and elapsed time (or number of samples) to achieve this.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about neural implementation.

claim: Downstream structures that control the arm must have access to the decision about both direction and confidence to control the initial reach and possibly revise the movement.
source: Of course, downstream structures that control the arm must have access to the decision about both direction and confidence to control the initial reach and possibly revise the movement.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental design and results.

claim: To explain the findings, it was assumed that choice and confidence are related but processed as if separate attributes, via a correspondence between decision variable and belief.
source: To explain our findings, we assumed that choice and confidence are related but processed as if separate attributes, via a correspondence between decision variable and belief.
evidence: This is a statement about the model assumptions.

claim: It is intriguing to think that the two dimensions (choice and confidence), which are bound together into a single action by the motor reach system in the task, could be dissociated in cognition and memory.
source: It is intriguing to think that the two dimensions, which are bound together into a single action by the motor reach system in our task, could be dissociated in cognition and memory.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about future research directions.

claim: Six naïve right-handed subjects, between the ages of 21 and 34, participated in this study.
source: Six naïve right-handed subjects, between the ages of 21 and 34, participated in this study.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the participants.

claim: The Cambridge Psychology Research Ethics Committee approved the experimental protocol.
source: The Cambridge Psychology Research Ethics Committee approved the experimental protocol, and subjects gave informed consent.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: Subjects gave informed consent.
source: The Cambridge Psychology Research Ethics Committee approved the experimental protocol, and subjects gave informed consent.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical procedures.

claim: Two of the subjects were excluded from the analyses based on poor task performance.
source: Two of the subjects were excluded from the analyses based on poor task performance (see below).
evidence: This is a statement about data exclusion.

claim: The evaluation of additional evidence may explain why confidence ratings are more strongly correlated with accuracy when they are reported with less time pressure.
source: The evaluation of additional evidence may explain why confidence ratings are more strongly correlated with accuracy when they are reported with less time pressure (Yu et al., 2015)
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by a citation.

claim: The evaluation of additional evidence may explain why some individuals appear to be better than others at discriminating correct from incorrect decisions.
source: and why some individuals appear to be better than others at discriminating correct from incorrect decisions (e.g. Ais et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by a citation.
